Front: Which baseline budget principles appear in Article 310 TFEU?
Back: All annual revenue and expenditure must appear in the budget; revenue and expenditure must balance; expenditure needs authorisation; implementation follows sound financial management; and the Union and Member States counter fraud.
Details: Budget-significant acts must be financeable within own-resources limits and the MFF. The annual budget is established by Parliament and the Council under Article 314.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Article 310(1)–(6) TFEU

Front: How does the Treaty describe financing through own resources?
Back: Without prejudice to other revenue, the Union budget is financed wholly from own resources. The Council unanimously adopts the own-resources decision after consulting Parliament, and Member States approve it under their constitutional requirements.
Details: The Union must provide itself the means needed for its objectives and policies. The decision may create or abolish categories of own resources; Parliament consents to implementing measures where the decision provides for them.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Article 311 TFEU

Front: What does the Multiannual Financial Framework do, and how is it adopted?
Back: It keeps Union expenditure orderly and within own-resource limits, sets annual commitment and payment ceilings, and lasts at least five years. The Council adopts it unanimously after Parliament's consent.
Details: The annual budget must comply with the MFF. The European Council may unanimously authorise qualified-majority voting for the Council's MFF regulation.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Article 312(1)–(5) TFEU

Front: Who proposes, adopts, implements, audits and discharges the annual EU budget?
Back: The Commission proposes; Parliament and the Council establish it; the Commission implements it with Member States; the Court of Auditors audits; and Parliament grants discharge to the Commission on a Council recommendation.
Details: This chain separates political adoption, executive implementation, external audit and democratic accountability. The financial year runs from 1 January to 31 December.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union

Front: What are DigComp 2.2's five digital-competence areas?
Back: Information and data literacy; communication and collaboration; digital content creation; safety; and problem solving.
Details: DigComp groups 21 competences into these areas. The first three map to particular activities and uses; safety and problem solving are transversal across digital activities.
Source title: DigComp 2.2: The Digital Competence Framework for Citizens
Source locator: Section 2, 'The Digital Competence Framework for Citizens', printed p. 8; Figure 3; table of contents, printed pp. I–II

Front: Which competences make up DigComp Area 1: Information and data literacy?
Back: 1.1 Browse, search and filter data, information and digital content; 1.2 evaluate them; 1.3 manage them.
Details: The area covers articulating information needs, locating and retrieving content, judging source relevance, and storing, organising and managing digital information and data.

Front: Which competences make up DigComp Area 2: Communication and collaboration?

Details: The framework couples tool choice and participation with attribution, collaborative processes, behavioural norms, diversity awareness, and control of one's digital presence and reputation.

Front: Which competences make up DigComp Area 3: Digital content creation?

Front: Which competences make up DigComp Area 4: Safety?

Front: Which competences make up DigComp Area 5: Problem solving?

Front: What practical drafting habits from the Commission's clear-writing guide reinforce the EUFTE anchors?

Back: 40 multiple-choice questions in 30 minutes, scored 0–40, with a pass mark of 20/40.
Details: The test assesses digital literacy in line with DigComp and draws from five stated areas. Its score contributes to ranking after the EU Knowledge Test is passed.
Source title: Consolidated Notice of Open Competition EPSO/AD/427/26 — Administrators (AD 5)
Source locator: Section 4.3.2(d) and Table 4, printed pp. 6–7

Front: What is the official format and pass mark of the EUFTE?
Back: 40 minutes, scored 0–10, with a pass mark of 5/10.
Details: Candidates answer assignment(s) using EU-related documentation released ahead of the test and supplied again during it. EPSO states that this is a written-communication test, not a language or factual-knowledge test.
Source title: Consolidated Notice of Open Competition EPSO/AD/427/26 — Administrators (AD 5)
Source locator: Section 4.3.2(e) and Table 5, printed p. 7

Front: How is the preliminary combined score weighted?
Back: Verbal reasoning 40%, EU Knowledge Test 30%, and digital skills 30%. Numerical and abstract reasoning are pass-only at this stage; EUFTE is not yet included.
Details: Only candidates who obtain all required pass scores have these results combined. The preliminary ranking determines whose EUFTE script and eligibility will be processed.
Source title: Consolidated Notice of Open Competition EPSO/AD/427/26 — Administrators (AD 5)
Source locator: Section 4.3.3(a), Table 6, printed p. 7; Section 4.3.3(b)(ii)–(iv), printed p. 8

Front: How is the final combined score weighted?
Back: Verbal reasoning 35%, EU Knowledge Test 25%, digital skills 25%, and EUFTE 15%. Numerical and abstract reasoning remain pass-only.
Details: EUFTE scoring and eligibility checks are normally limited to candidates taken in preliminary-rank order, in principle no more than 1.5 times the 1,490 successful candidates sought, subject to equal scores and a Selection Board increase.
Source title: Consolidated Notice of Open Competition EPSO/AD/427/26 — Administrators (AD 5)
Source locator: Section 4.3.3(a), Table 6, printed p. 7; Section 4.3.3(b)(iv)–(vii), printed pp. 8–9

Front: What are the European Parliament's core Treaty functions?
Back: Jointly with the Council, it exercises legislative and budgetary functions. It also exercises political control and consultation and elects the Commission President.
Details: Members represent Union citizens and are elected every five years by direct universal suffrage in a free and secret ballot.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union
Source locator: Article 14(1)–(4) TEU

Front: What does the European Council do—and what does it not do?
Back: It gives the Union development impetus and defines general political directions and priorities. It does not exercise legislative functions.
Details: It comprises the Member States' heads of state or government, its President and the Commission President; the High Representative takes part. Unless the Treaties say otherwise, it decides by consensus.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union
Source locator: Article 15(1)–(4) TEU

Front: What are the Council's core functions and default voting rule?
Back: Jointly with Parliament, it exercises legislative and budgetary functions; it also makes policy and coordinates. It acts by qualified majority unless the Treaties provide otherwise.
Details: The ordinary double-majority threshold is at least 55% of Council members, at least 15, representing at least 65% of the Union population; a blocking minority normally needs at least four members.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union
Source locator: Article 16(1)–(4) TEU

Front: What are the Commission's core Treaty functions?
Back: Promote the Union's general interest; initiate action; ensure Treaty and Union-law application under Court control; execute the budget; manage programmes; and perform coordinating, executive and management functions.
Details: Except where the Treaties provide otherwise, Union legislative acts are adopted on a Commission proposal. Outside CFSP and other exceptions, the Commission also ensures external representation and initiates annual and multiannual programming.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union
Source locator: Article 17(1)–(3) TEU

Front: What is the CJEU's core mission and what main kinds of ruling does it give?
Back: It ensures that the law is observed in interpreting and applying the Treaties. It rules on actions, gives preliminary rulings requested by national courts on Union-law interpretation or act validity, and handles other Treaty cases.
Details: The CJEU includes the Court of Justice, the General Court and any specialised courts. Member States must provide remedies sufficient for effective legal protection in Union-law fields.
Topic: Court of Justice of the European Union
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union
Source locator: Article 19(1)–(3) TEU

Front: What is the ESCB's primary objective, and what special authority does the ECB have over the euro?
Back: The ESCB's primary objective is price stability. The ECB alone may authorise issuance of the euro and must be independent in exercising its powers and managing its finances.
Details: The ECB and national central banks form the ESCB; the ECB and central banks of euro-area Member States form the Eurosystem and conduct Union monetary policy.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Article 282(1)–(3) TFEU

Front: What does the European Court of Auditors do?
Back: It carries out the Union's audit: examining revenue and expenditure, the reliability of accounts, the legality and regularity of underlying transactions, and whether financial management is sound.
Details: It provides Parliament and the Council with a statement of assurance and assists them in controlling budget implementation. Its members must be completely independent in performing their duties.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Articles 285 and 287(1)–(2) TFEU

Front: What are the defining legal effects of an EU regulation?
Back: It has general application, is binding in its entirety, and is directly applicable in every Member State.
Details: Article 288 combines three characteristics for the regulation form: general application, full binding force and direct applicability throughout the Member States.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Article 288, second paragraph, TFEU

Front: What are the defining legal effects of an EU directive?
Back: It binds each Member State to which it is addressed as to the result, while leaving national authorities the choice of form and methods.
Details: A directive therefore differs from a regulation: Article 288 builds national implementation choices into the directive form.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Article 288, third paragraph, TFEU

Front: How do decisions, recommendations and opinions differ under Article 288 TFEU?
Back: A decision is binding in its entirety; if it names addressees, it binds only them. Recommendations and opinions have no binding force.
Details: All five Article 288 forms—regulations, directives, decisions, recommendations and opinions—are Union legal acts, but only the first three are described there as binding.
Tags: decision eu-knowledge legal-acts opinion recommendation tfeu
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Article 288, fourth and fifth paragraphs, TFEU

Front: What defines the ordinary legislative procedure?
Back: Parliament and the Council jointly adopt a regulation, directive or decision on a Commission proposal, following the readings and possible conciliation set out in Article 294 TFEU.
Details: At first reading Parliament adopts a position. If the Council approves it, the act is adopted; otherwise the Council sends its own position back. Later disagreement can lead to a second reading and a Conciliation Committee.
Tags: commission council eu-knowledge olp parliament tfeu
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Articles 289(1) and 294(1)–(10) TFEU

Front: What is the difference between delegated and implementing acts?
Back: A delegated act is a Commission non-legislative act of general application that supplements or amends non-essential elements of legislation. An implementing act supplies uniform conditions for implementing a binding Union act, usually through Commission powers.
Details: Legislation must define delegation objectives, scope and duration; Parliament or Council can revoke or object under the set conditions. Member States normally implement Union acts, but uniformity can justify conferred implementing powers.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Articles 290(1)–(3) and 291(1)–(4) TFEU

Front: Is this deck the official EU Knowledge Test syllabus?
Back: No. The official source pack is still pending. EPSO says references to the materials used to develop the test will be published approximately two months before the test date.
Details: Use these cards as authoritative background only. Once EPSO publishes the source references, replace or revalidate every EU-knowledge card against that pack; do not infer official scope from this provisional deck.
Source title: EU Knowledge Test material available 2 months before test

Front: What are the three pillars of the European Council's Strategic Agenda 2024–2029?
Back: A free and democratic Europe; a strong and secure Europe; and a prosperous and competitive Europe.
Details: The European Council agreed the agenda on 27 June 2024. It sets strategic orientations for the institutional cycle and guides the institutions; it is distinct from the Commission's seven political priorities.
Source title: Strategic agenda 2024–2029
Source locator: Introductory section and headings 'A free and democratic Europe', 'A strong and secure Europe', 'A prosperous and competitive Europe'

Front: What are the Commission's seven priorities for 2024–2029?
Back: Sustainable prosperity and competitiveness; defence and security; people, society and the social model; quality of life—food security, water and nature; democracy and values; a global Europe; and delivering together while preparing the Union's future.
Details: These seven Commission priorities operationalise the political programme for the current mandate. Their wording and supporting initiatives are time-sensitive and should be rechecked against the live Commission page.
Source title: Commission's priorities 2024–2029
Source locator: Seven priority headings under 'Commission’s priorities'

Front: Which values found the European Union under Article 2 TEU?
Back: Human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law, and respect for human rights, including minority rights.
Details: Article 2 also describes the Member-State society in which these values are common: pluralism, non-discrimination, tolerance, justice, solidarity, and equality between women and men prevail.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union
Source locator: Article 2 TEU

Front: What core objectives does Article 3 TEU set for the Union?
Back: Promote peace, its values and peoples' well-being; provide an area of freedom, security and justice; establish an internal market; pursue sustainable development and cohesion; establish economic and monetary union with the euro; and uphold its values and interests in the wider world.
Details: The article expands these objectives with balanced growth, price stability, a highly competitive social market economy, social progress, environmental protection, scientific advance, anti-discrimination, solidarity, cultural and linguistic diversity, human rights and international law.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union
Source locator: Article 3(1)–(6) TEU

Front: How do conferral, subsidiarity and proportionality differ?
Back: Conferral limits the Union to competences granted by the Treaties. Subsidiarity asks, outside exclusive competence, whether objectives are better achieved at Union level. Proportionality limits Union action to what is necessary for Treaty objectives.
Details: Competences not conferred remain with Member States. Subsidiarity compares achievement at central, regional and local Member-State levels with the scale or effects of Union action; proportionality governs both content and form.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union
Source locator: Article 5(1)–(4) TEU

Front: What does sincere cooperation require under Article 4(3) TEU?
Back: The Union and Member States must assist each other, in full mutual respect, in carrying out Treaty tasks. Member States must fulfil Union obligations, facilitate Union tasks and avoid measures that could jeopardise Union objectives.
Details: The same article also protects Member-State equality, national identities and essential State functions; national security remains each Member State's sole responsibility.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union
Source locator: Article 4(1)–(3) TEU

Front: How are citizens and Member States represented democratically at Union level?
Back: Citizens are directly represented in the European Parliament. Member States are represented by their heads in the European Council and by their governments in the Council, with those governments democratically accountable nationally.
Details: Article 10 TEU grounds the Union in representative democracy and requires decisions to be taken as openly and as closely as possible to citizens. Article 9 says Union citizenship is additional to, not a replacement for, national citizenship.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union
Source locator: Articles 9 and 10(1)–(4) TEU

Front: Which seven bodies are Union institutions under Article 13 TEU?
Back: European Parliament; European Council; Council; European Commission; Court of Justice of the European Union; European Central Bank; and Court of Auditors.
Details: Each institution must act within its conferred powers and the Treaty procedures, conditions and objectives. The institutions practise mutual sincere cooperation. The EESC and Committee of the Regions are advisory bodies, not institutions in this list.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union
Source locator: Article 13(1)–(4) TEU

Front: How do exclusive, shared and supporting Union competences operate?
Back: Exclusive: only the Union legislates, unless it empowers Member States or they implement Union acts. Shared: both may legislate, but Member-State scope recedes when the Union acts. Supporting: the Union supports, coordinates or supplements without superseding Member-State competence or harmonising national law.
Details: These are categories of power, not a ranking of policy importance. The detailed scope always depends on the Treaty legal basis for the particular field.
Tags: competences eu-knowledge exclusive shared supporting tfeu
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Article 2(1), 2(2) and 2(5) TFEU

Front: Which five policy areas are expressly exclusive Union competences?
Back: Customs union; internal-market competition rules; monetary policy for euro-area Member States; conservation of marine biological resources under the common fisheries policy; and common commercial policy.
Details: Article 3(2) separately makes conclusion of certain international agreements an exclusive competence when specified Treaty conditions are met.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Article 3(1)–(2) TFEU

Front: Which principal areas are shared competences under Article 4(2) TFEU?
Back: Internal market; defined aspects of social policy; cohesion; agriculture and fisheries except marine-resource conservation; environment; consumer protection; transport; trans-European networks; energy; freedom, security and justice; and defined common public-health safety concerns.
Details: Research, technological development and space, plus development cooperation and humanitarian aid, have special parallel-action rules in Article 4(3)–(4): Union action does not prevent Member-State action.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Article 4(1)–(4) TFEU

Front: Which areas can the Union support, coordinate or supplement under Article 6 TFEU?
Back: Human health protection and improvement; industry; culture; tourism; education, vocational training, youth and sport; civil protection; and administrative cooperation.
Details: These supporting actions do not supersede Member-State competence, and binding Union acts based on supporting competences may not harmonise Member-State laws or regulations.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Articles 2(5) and 6 TFEU

Front: What core citizenship rights are listed in Article 20(2) TFEU?
Back: Free movement and residence; voting and standing in European Parliament and municipal elections in the Member State of residence; consular protection by another Member State abroad when one's own is unrepresented; and petition, Ombudsman and Treaty-language communication rights.
Details: Union citizenship belongs to every person holding Member-State nationality. It is additional to, not a replacement for, national citizenship, and rights operate under Treaty and legislative conditions and limits.
Source title: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Source locator: Article 20(1)–(2) TFEU
